cssig

Composite selection signals (CSS) for detecting signatures of selection.

An R implementation of the CSS method of Randhawa, Khatkar, Thomson and Raadsma.

# install
remotes::install_github("msk99/cssig")                    # add build_vignettes = TRUE for vignettes

# run on the bundled example data
library(cssig)
data(css_sim_small)

x   <- css_input(css_sim_small, tests = c(fst = "high", xpehh = "high", ddaf = "high"))
res <- css(x) |> css_smooth() |> css_threshold(top = 0.001)
reg <- css_regions(res)

summary(reg)
css_manhattan(res, regions = reg)

# help
?css
vignette("cssig")

What this package is

Genome scans for selection rely on statistics like FST, XP-EHH and ΔDAF. Each is sensitive to a different aspect of a selective sweep, and none is decisive on its own — run three tests on the same data and you typically get three partly overlapping answers.

CSS combines them into a single non-parametric index. Each constituent test is ranked genome-wide, the ranks become normal quantiles, and the quantiles are averaged at every SNP. A locus where several tests agree is amplified; a locus where only one test is extreme is pulled back toward the genome-wide average.

cssig takes pre-computed constituent statistics and does everything downstream of them: the CSS statistic, sliding-window smoothing, empirical thresholds, region calling, FDR, reciprocal (signed) cohort contrasts, and plots.

The method

For test i at SNP j, with m tests and n SNPs:

Step Operation
1 rank genome-wide R[j,i] = rank(T[,i])
2 fractional rank R'[j,i] = R[j,i] / (n + 1)
3 normal quantile Z[j,i] = qnorm(R'[j,i])
4 mean across tests Zbar[j] = mean(Z[j,])
5 p-value p[j] = 1 - pnorm(sqrt(m) * Zbar[j])
6 CSS -log10(p[j])

Scope

In scope — the CSS statistic and everything after it, plus the constituents that are one-liners from allele frequencies (css_fst(), css_ddaf(), css_dsaf()).

Out of scope — VCF/PLINK parsing, phasing, imputation, and XP-EHH computation. Use rehh, selscan or hapbin for haplotype statistics and bring the output here; read_rehh_xpehh() and read_selscan_xpehh() handle the coercion.

Installation

Requires R >= 4.1, and remotes for the install command at the top of this page.

install_github() skips vignettes by default, which is why vignette("cssig") can report “not found” — add build_vignettes = TRUE (it needs knitr and rmarkdown). Both vignettes are also readable on GitHub without installing: cssig.Rmd and simulation.Rmd.

Or from a local source tree:

git clone https://github.com/msk99/cssig.git
R CMD INSTALL cssig

Hard dependencies are only data.table (>= 1.15) and ggplot2. Optional extras, each needed for one feature:

install.packages(c("fdrtool",  # css_fdr(method = "fdrtool" / "isotonic")
                   "circlize", # css_circos()
                   "rehh"))    # computing XP-EHH in the first place

scrm and rehh are additionally needed only to regenerate the bundled example data from data-raw/; they are never loaded by the installed package.

Usage

1. Prepare the input

You need one row per SNP: a chromosome, a position, and one numeric column per constituent test.

head(css_sim_small[, .(chr, pos, fst, xpehh, ddaf)])

css_input() validates it and records, per test, which direction means more evidence of selection:

x <- css_input(my_stats,
               chr = "chr", pos = "pos", snp = "rsid",
               tests = c(fst = "high", xpehh = "high", ddaf = "high"))
direction Meaning Typical use
"high" use as-is FST; XP-EHH with the selected population as target; ΔDAF as selected − reference
"low" negate before ranking Tajima’s D, π ratios
"abs" use magnitude only a signed test whose sign you do not trust

It accepts a data.frame, tibble, data.table or matrix, and returns a data.table keyed on (chr, pos).

Two details that surprise people:

  • chr comes back as a factor, not character. That is deliberate: as character, a keyed table sorts 1, 10, 2, 22, X, which would scramble the Manhattan axis and the order of called regions. The factor carries genomic order, so you get 1, 2, 10, 22, X. Filtering is unaffected — both chr == "2" and chr == 2 work.
  • A column named snp is picked up automatically. Pass snp = "rsid" for a differently named one; with neither, identifiers of the form "chr:pos" are generated.

If your tests come from different tools — and so cover slightly different SNP sets — join them explicitly rather than hoping they line up:

a <- data.frame(chr = 1, pos = c(100, 200, 300), fst   = c(0.10, 0.22, 0.31))
b <- data.frame(chr = 1, pos = c(200, 300, 400), xpehh = c(1.1, 2.2, 0.4))

css_merge_tests(fst = a, xpehh = b, all = FALSE)   # FALSE = complete cases only
#> Merged 2 tests on (chr, pos), keeping the intersection: 2 SNPs.
#>   fst                3 in ->       2 retained (66.7%)
#>   xpehh              3 in ->       2 retained (66.7%)
#>       chr   pos   fst xpehh
#>    <char> <num> <num> <num>
#> 1:      1   200  0.22   1.1
#> 2:      1   300  0.31   2.2

Use all = TRUE to keep the union instead, leaving NA where a test is missing. The retention report exists because silent SNP loss at this step is the commonest way a scan goes quietly wrong.

2. Getting the constituent statistics

From allele counts and frequencies, in-package:

fst  <- css_fst(count1 = derived_selected, n1 = n_ind_selected,
                count2 = derived_reference, n2 = n_ind_reference)
ddaf <- css_ddaf(daf_selected, daf_reference)   # needs ancestral allele
dsaf <- css_dsaf(freq_selected, freq_reference) # ancestral-free alternative

XP-EHH needs phased haplotypes, so it comes from elsewhere:

# rehh
sel <- rehh::scan_hh(hh_selected);  ref <- rehh::scan_hh(hh_reference)
xp  <- read_rehh_xpehh(rehh::ies2xpehh(sel, ref))

# selscan
xp  <- read_selscan_xpehh("chr1.xpehh.out", chr = 1)

3. Run the pipeline 

res <- css(x)                                          # the CSS statistic
res <- css_smooth(res, half_width = 5e5, min_snps = 5) # 1 Mb sliding window
res <- css_threshold(res, top = 0.001)                 # empirical top 0.1%

Useful arguments:

Function Argument Default Notes
css() ties "average" passed to data.table::frank()
na_action "pairwise" uses each SNP’s own m; "omit" for strict complete cases
weights NULL equal weights = the published method
css_smooth() half_width 5e5 half-width in bp, so 1 Mb total
min_snps 5 sparser windows are masked
cols NULL also smooth the constituent tests, for comparison plots
css_threshold() top 0.001 top 0.1%, as in both papers
top2 0.01 the more permissive tier used by method = "flank"

4. Call regions

Two published rules, one from each paper:

css_regions(res, method = "cluster")  # 2014: >= 3 significant SNPs in a window
css_regions(res, method = "flank")    # 2015: 1 top-0.1% SNP + >= 5 top-1% neighbours

Both return one row per region with the span, peak SNP, and — when the constituent tests are still attached — how many SNPs in each test’s own top fraction fall inside. That last part is how you tell a signal supported by several tests from one driven by a single test.

start_padded / end_padded carry the ±0.5 Mb both papers add for gene mining. The padding is never folded into start / end, so region boundaries are not silently inflated.

5. FDR 

res <- css_fdr(res, method = "BH")        # default, no extra dependency
res <- css_fdr(res, method = "fdrtool")   # the route used in the 2014 paper

Run this before css_smooth(). Smoothing averages −log10(p) over neighbouring SNPs, and the result is no longer a p-value; css_fdr() refuses smoothed input rather than returning numbers that look like q-values but are not. See the caveat in Things worth knowing below.

6. Reciprocal (signed) analysis

The 2015 paper compares two cohorts in both directions, so a signal’s sign says which cohort carries it:

fwd <- css_input(dat,      tests = c(fst = "high", xpehh = "high", ddaf = "high"))
rev <- css_input(dat_swapped, tests = c(fst = "high", xpehh = "high", ddaf = "high"))
recip <- css_reciprocal(fwd, rev, labels = c("large", "small"))
css_manhattan_mirror(recip)

7. Weighting the constituents

Off by default, because equal weights are the published method. Use it when you have a stated reason to trust one test less — not by tuning until the answer improves:

res <- css(x, weights = c(fst = 1, xpehh = 1, ddaf = 0.25))

weights = c(1,1,1) reproduces the unweighted statistic exactly, and print() flags a weighted run. Worked example with known truth in vignette("simulation").

8. Plots

Every plot function returns a ggplot object you can modify, except css_circos(), which draws with circlize.

Function What it shows
css_manhattan() genome-wide CSS, alternating chromosomes, threshold line
css_manhattan_mirror() two reciprocal directions above and below zero
css_chrom_plot() one chromosome: raw points, smoothed line, gene marks
css_region_plot() one region, faceted into CSS + each constituent test
css_qq(), css_pdist() p-value calibration
css_fdr_density() q-values inside called regions vs the rest of the genome
css_test_cor() correlation among constituents and CSS
css_circos() circular multi-track genome plot
css_theme(), css_genome_coords() building blocks for custom plots

Things worth knowing

CSS depends only on ranks. Standardising XP-EHH or ΔDAF to N(0,1), as both papers do, leaves CSS exactly unchanged — it matters only for plotting. Any strictly increasing transform of a constituent gives identical CSS.

Ranks are genome-wide. Adding or removing SNPs changes every SNP’s score, so keep the SNP set fixed when comparing runs.

The CSS p-value is not calibrated on real data. The formula assumes the constituent tests are independent. They are not, and the correlation is not always positive: in the bundled css_sim, XP-EHH and ΔDAF correlate at about −0.32, which deflates the variance of Zbar (observed sd 0.90 rather than 1.00; permuting each test restores it to 1.00). Treat CSS as a ranking, not a tail probability. This is why both papers threshold on the empirical top 0.1% rather than on a p-value, and why q-values deserve a look at css_qq() first.

Pipeline stages modify their object by reference. data.table semantics, so a multi-million-row table is never copied between stages:

res <- css(x)
"css" %in% names(x)   # TRUE -- x and res are the same object

Your original input is always safe — css_input() copies it once on the way in — but if you want each stage to return a fresh copy, pass .copy = TRUE.

Bundled data

Simulated, and generated the slow way: a population is simulated and the statistics are computed from it, rather than the statistics being drawn from a distribution. That matters because the three tests are correlated through a shared genealogy, and inventing that correlation would make any demonstration circular.

Object Contents
css_sim 46,976 SNPs × 29 bovine autosomes, 8 vs 8 breeds, 800 animals
css_sim_small 5,502 SNPs on chromosomes 1–2, for fast examples
css_sim_truth the 7 known signatures: 6 sweeps and one deliberate false positive

These data are simulated and describe no real animal, breed or genome. The generating scripts are in data-raw/; see ?css_sim.

Path What it is

data-raw/ scripts that regenerate them (design notes)

Troubleshooting

vignette("cssig") says “not found”. install_github() does not build vignettes unless asked. Reinstall with build_vignettes = TRUE (see Installation), or read them on GitHub.

Plots crash R, or fail with no applicable method for 'depth', on macOS. Symptoms are a session killed by zsh: trace trap, or an error followed by can't shut down a locked device. Once it happens the graphics device is wedged and every later plot fails, so restart R first.

Then work out which of two situations you are in:

plot(1:10)                                                  # base graphics
print(ggplot2::ggplot(mtcars, ggplot2::aes(wt, mpg)) + ggplot2::geom_point())
  • Those also fail — R’s on-screen Quartz device is at fault, not this package. A macOS crash report will show CFRelease inside -[QuartzCocoaView drawRect:] with no package code on the stack. Write plots to files instead, or use RStudio or Positron, which use a different device.
  • Those succeed but a cssig plot still fails — that is a bug here; please open an issue with your sessionInfo(). Version 1.0.0 removed the infinite rectangle bounds that were the likeliest trigger, so make sure you are current.

Either way, writing to a file is a reliable workaround:

ggplot2::ggsave("manhattan.png", css_manhattan(res, regions = reg),
                width = 10, height = 4, dpi = 150)
